entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen30816" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen30817" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen30817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30818" type="x-p"/> This chapter was added after Jeremiah's time probably by Ezra, after the return from the captivity, of which it gives a short account, nearly the same as in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18-2Kgs.24.20">2Kgs 24:18-20</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18-2Kgs.24.20">2Kgs 24:18-20</reference>. It is very properly subjoined to the preceding prophecies, in order to show how exactly they were fulfilled. It likewise forms a proper introduction to the following Lamentations, as it gives an account of the mournful events which gave rise to them. Zedekiah's evil reign and rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.1-Jer.52.3">Jer 52:1-3</reference>. Jerusalem is taken by the Chaldeans after a siege of eighteen months, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.4-Jer.52.7">Jer 52:4-7</reference>. Zedekiah pursued and taken in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army dispersed, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.8">Jer 52:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.9">Jer 52:9</reference>. The king's sons and all the princes of Judah slain in Riblah, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.10">Jer 52:10</reference>. Zedekiah has his eyes put out by order of the Chaldean monarch; and is afterward bound in chains, carried to Babylon, and imprisoned for life, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.11">Jer 52:11</reference>. Nebuzar-adan, the captain of the guard, burns and spoils the city and temple, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12-Jer.52.19">Jer 52:12-19</reference>. The two pillars of the temple, with their dimensions and ornaments, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.20-Jer.52.23">Jer 52:20-23</reference>. The officers of the temple, and several others, carried away captives into Babylon, and then slain by order of Nebuchadnezzar, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.24-Jer.52.27">Jer 52:24-27</reference>. The number of Jews that Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive in the seventh year of his reign, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.28">Jer 52:28</reference>; in his eighteenth year, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.29">Jer 52:29</reference>; and in his twenty-third year, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.30">Jer 52:30</reference>. Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, in the year of his accession to the throne of Babylon, (which was in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity, and the one hundred and ninety-first from the building of Rome, according to the computation of Varro), orders Jehoiachin to be taken out of prison, and treats him kindly for the remainder of his life, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.31-Jer.52.34">Jer 52:31-34</reference>. <div eID="gen30818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30819" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen30819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30820" type="x-p"/> Zedekiah was one and twenty years old - See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.18">2Kgs 24:18</reference>.
entries.content_plain: Introduction This chapter was added after Jeremiah's time probably by Ezra, after the return from the captivity, of which it gives a short account, nearly the same as in 2Kgs 24:18-20 , and 2Kgs 24:18-20 . It is very properly subjoined to the preceding prophecies, in order to show how exactly they were fulfilled. It likewise forms a proper introduction to the following Lamentations, as it gives an account of the mournful events which gave rise to them. Zedekiah's evil reign and rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, Jer 52:1-3 . Jerusalem is taken by the Chaldeans after a siege of eighteen months, Jer 52:4-7 . Zedekiah pursued and taken in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army dispersed, Jer 52:8 , Jer 52:9 . The king's sons and all the princes of Judah slain in Riblah, Jer 52:10 . Zedekiah has his eyes put out by order of the Chaldean monarch; and is afterward bound in chains, carried to Babylon, and imprisoned for life, Jer 52:11 . Nebuzar-adan, the captain of the guard, burns and spoils the city and temple, Jer 52:12-19 . The two pillars of the temple, with their dimensions and ornaments, Jer 52:20-23 . The officers of the temple, and several others, carried away captives into Babylon, and then slain by order of Nebuchadnezzar, Jer 52:24-27 . The number of Jews that Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive in the seventh year of his reign, Jer 52:28 ; in his eighteenth year, Jer 52:29 ; and in his twenty-third year, Jer 52:30 . Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, in the year of his accession to the throne of Babylon, (which was in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity, and the one hundred and ninety-first from the building of Rome, according to the computation of Varro), orders Jehoiachin to be taken out of prison, and treats him kindly for the remainder of his life, Jer 52:31-34 . entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen30837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30838" type="x-p"/> On these verses Dr. Blayney has some sensible remarks; I will extract the substance. These verses are not inserted in 2 Kings 25. Are we to conclude from these verses that the whole number of the Jews which Nebuchadnezzar, in all his expeditions, carried away, was no more than four thousand six hundred? This cannot be true; for he carried away more than twice that number at one time and this is expressly said to have been in the eighth year of his reign, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12-2Kgs.24.16">2Kgs 24:12-16</reference>. Before that time he had carried off a number of captives from Jerusalem, in the first year of his reign, among whom were Daniel and his companions, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.3-Dan.1.6">Dan 1:3-6</reference>. These are confessedly not noticed here. And as the taking and burning of Jerusalem is in this very chapter said to have been in the fourth and fifth months of the nineteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, those who were carried into captivity at the date of those events cannot possibly be the same with those that are said to be carried away either in the eighteenth or twenty-third year of that prince. Nor, indeed, is it credible that the number carried away at the time that the city was taken, and the whole country reduced, could be so few as eight hundred and thirty-two, (see <reference osisRef="Jer.52.29">Jer 52:29</reference>); supposing a mistake in the date of the year, which some are willing to do without sufficient grounds. <div eID="gen30838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30839" type="x-p"/> Here then we have three deportations, and those the most considerable ones, in the first, in the eighth, and nineteenth years of Nebuchadnezzar, sufficiently distinguished from those in the seventh, eighteenth, and twenty-third years. So that it seems most reasonable to conclude with Abp. Usher, in Chronologia Sacra, that by the latter three the historian meant to point out deportations of a minor kind, not elsewhere noticed in direct terms in Scripture. <div eID="gen30839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30840" type="x-p"/> The first of these, said to have been in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, was one of those that had been picked up in several parts of Judah by the band of Chaldeans, Syrians, and others, whom the king of Babylon sent against the land previously to his own coming, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.2">2Kgs 24:2</reference>. <div eID="gen30840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30841" type="x-p"/> That in the eighteenth year corresponds with the time when the Chaldean army broke off the siege before Jerusalem, and marched to meet the Egyptian army, at which time they might think it proper to send off the prisoners that were in camp, under a guard to Babylon. <div eID="gen30841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30842" type="x-p"/> And the last, in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, was when that monarch, being engaged in the siege of Tyre, sent off Nebuzaradan against the Moabites, Ammonites, and other neighboring nations, who at the same time carried away the gleanings of Jews that remained in their own land, amounting in all to no more than seven hundred and forty-five. <div eID="gen30842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30843" type="x-p"/> Josephus speaks of this expedition against the Moabites and Ammonites, which he places in the twenty-third year or Nebuchadnezzar; but mentions nothing done in the land of Israel at that time. Only he says that after the conquest of those nations, Nebuchadnezzar carried his victorious arms against Egypt, which he in some measure reduced, and carried the Jews whom he found there captives to Babylon. But the Egyptian expedition was not till the twenty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, i.e., the thirty-fifth of Nebuchadnezzar, as may be collected from <reference osisRef="Eze.29.17">Eze 29:17</reference>; so that those who were carried away in the twenty-third year were not from Egypt, but were, as before observed, the few Jews that remained in the land of Judah.
entries.content_plain: Verse 28 On these verses Dr. Blayney has some sensible remarks; I will extract the substance. These verses are not inserted in 2 Kings 25. Are we to conclude from these verses that the whole number of the Jews which Nebuchadnezzar, in all his expeditions, carried away, was no more than four thousand six hundred? This cannot be true; for he carried away more than twice that number at one time and this is expressly said to have been in the eighth year of his reign, 2Kgs 24:12-16 . Before that time he had carried off a number of captives from Jerusalem, in the first year of his reign, among whom were Daniel and his companions, Dan 1:3-6 . These are confessedly not noticed here. And as the taking and burning of Jerusalem is in this very chapter said to have been in the fourth and fifth months of the nineteenth year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, those who were carried into captivity at the date of those events cannot possibly be the same with those that are said to be carried away either in the eighteenth or twenty-third year of that prince. Here then we have three deportations, and those the most considerable ones, in the first, in the eighth, and nineteenth years of Nebuchadnezzar, sufficiently distinguished from those in the seventh, eighteenth, and twenty-third years. So that it seems most reasonable to conclude with Abp. Usher, in Chronologia Sacra, that by the latter three the historian meant to point out deportations of a minor kind, not elsewhere noticed in direct terms in Scripture. The first of these, said to have been in the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, was one of those that had been picked up in several parts of Judah by the band of Chaldeans, Syrians, and others, whom the king of Babylon sent against the land previously to his own coming, 2Kgs 24:2 . That in the eighteenth year corresponds with the time when the Chaldean army broke off the siege before Jerusalem, and marched to meet the Egyptian army, at which time they might think it proper to send off the prisoners that were in camp, under a guard to Babylon. And the last, in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, was when that monarch, being engaged in the siege of Tyre, sent off Nebuzaradan against the Moabites, Ammonites, and other neighboring nations, who at the same time carried away the gleanings of Jews that remained in their own land, amounting in all to no more than seven hundred and forty-five. Josephus speaks of this expedition against the Moabites and Ammonites, which he places in the twenty-third year or Nebuchadnezzar; but mentions nothing done in the land of Israel at that time. Only he says that after the conquest of those nations, Nebuchadnezzar carried his victorious arms against Egypt, which he in some measure reduced, and carried the Jews whom he found there captives to Babylon. entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen30843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30844" type="x-p"/> In the twelfth month - Answering nearly to our twenty-fifth of April, A.M. 3442. <div eID="gen30844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30845" type="x-p"/> Lifted up the head of Jehoiachin - This phrase is taken from <reference osisRef="Gen.40.13">Gen 40:13</reference>. It is founded on the observation that those who are in sorrow hold down their heads, and when they are comforted, or the cause of their sorrow removed, they lift up their heads. The Hebrew phrase, lift up the head, signifies to comfort, cheer, make happy.

entries.reader_content_plain: Verse 33 And changed his prison garments - That is, Jehoiachin changed his own garments, that he might be suited in that respect to the state of his elevation. Kings also, in token of favor, gave caftans or robes to those whom they wish to honor. And he did continually eat bread before him - Was a constant guest at the king's table.

navigation_sections.title: Introduction
navigation_sections.content_plain: Introduction This chapter was added after Jeremiah's time probably by Ezra, after the return from the captivity, of which it gives a short account, nearly the same as in 2Kgs 24:18-20 , and 2Kgs 24:18-20 . It is very properly subjoined to the preceding prophecies, in order to show how exactly they were fulfilled. It likewise forms a proper introduction to the following Lamentations, as it gives an account of the mournful events which gave rise to them. Zedekiah's evil reign and rebellion against Nebuchadnezzar, Jer 52:1-3 . Jerusalem is taken by the Chaldeans after a siege of eighteen months, Jer 52:4-7 . Zedekiah pursued and taken in the plains of Jericho, and his whole army dispersed, Jer 52:8 , Jer 52:9 . The king's sons and all the princes of Judah slain in Riblah, Jer 52:10 . Zedekiah has his eyes put out by order of the Chaldean monarch; and is afterward bound in chains, carried to Babylon, and imprisoned for life, Jer 52:11 . Nebuzar-adan, the captain of the guard, burns and spoils the city and temple, Jer 52:12-19 . The two pillars of the temple, with their dimensions and ornaments, Jer 52:20-23 . The officers of the temple, and several others, carried away captives into Babylon, and then slain by order of Nebuchadnezzar, Jer 52:24-27 . The number of Jews that Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive in the seventh year of his reign, Jer 52:28 ; in his eighteenth year, Jer 52:29 ; and in his twenty-third year, Jer 52:30 . Evil-merodach, the son of Nebuchadnezzar, in the year of his accession to the throne of Babylon, (which was in the thirty-seventh year of the captivity, and the one hundred and ninety-first from the building of Rome, according to the computation of Varro), orders Jehoiachin to be taken out of prison, and treats him kindly for the remainder of his life, Jer 52:31-34 .
